facts.statement: The genus Navajosuchus was named in 1942 by the paleontologist Charles C. Mook.
facts.quote: It was named in 1942 by Charles C. Mook

facts.statement: Fossils of Navajosuchus have been discovered in the Nacimiento Formation within the San Juan Basin of New Mexico, United States.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been found in the Paleocene-age Nacimiento Formation of the San Juan Basin, New Mexico (United States)

facts.statement: Navajosuchus was the most abundant crocodilian in the Nacimiento Formation, appearing in both the Puercan and Torrejonian faunal assemblages.
facts.quote: It was the most common Nacimiento Formation crocodilian, found in both the Puercan and Torrejonian faunal assemblages

facts.statement: Navajosuchus likely lived as a generalized predator on the floodplains of the Nacimiento Formation.
facts.quote: Under whichever name is used, this animal would have been a generalized predator of the Nacimiento floodplains

facts.statement: Scientists disagree on the precise classification of Navajosuchus within the group Alligatoroidea.
facts.quote: The precise placement of Navajosuchus within Alligatoroidea is disputed

facts.statement: Some research suggests Navajosuchus is a basal member of the family Alligatoridae, specifically within the subgroup Alligatorinae.
facts.quote: Some studies have shown it as a basal member of Alligatoridae, within the stem-based group Alligatorinae

facts.statement: Other studies propose that Navajosuchus belongs outside Alligatoridae and Alligatorinae, instead placing it as a basal member of the clade Globidonta.
facts.quote: Alternatively, other studies have recovered Navajosuchus outside of Alligatoridae and Alligatorinae, as a basal member of Alligatoroidea within the clade Globidonta

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database classifies Navajosuchus as a member of the parent group Alligatorinae.
Navajosuchus is classified within the family Alligatoridae.
Navajosuchus lived from the Danian to the Selandian stages, approximately 66 to 60.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Danian to Selandian (66 to 60.9 million years ago)
